cd /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek
gh issue comment 65 --body 'Correcting myself in the comment above. I wrote that `AGENTS.md` being
LF-only means "a CRLF conversion would not break" the new count check,
on the reasoning that the check flattens line breaks. **That is wrong,
and I checked it this time rather than reasoning about it.**

The flattening is `gsub(/[ \t]+/, " ", s)`. A `\r` is neither a space
nor a tab, so it survives and lands inside the phrase wherever the
phrase wraps. Converting `AGENTS.md` to CRLF drops the count from 4 to
2 — the two occurrences that wrap stop matching, the two that sit whole
on one line survive:

```
$ sed -i "s/$/\r/" AGENTS.md && tests/instructions.sh .
FAIL: AGENTS.md states the finding standard 2 times, expected 4 -- ...
```

It fails loudly rather than passing silently, so nothing is hidden and
the check is not dangerous. But the mitigation I claimed is not there,
and the reason to want an LF assertion is stronger than I said, not
weaker: today a CRLF conversion produces a red build with a message
about step wording, which points an editor at the wrong thing entirely.

`.gitattributes` currently covers only `tests/golden/*.txt`.

Found by `verifier`, which built the CRLF case instead of accepting the
claim.'
gh issue create --title "instructions.sh compares unvalidated command output as numbers in three places" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Problem

`tests/instructions.sh` captures command output and compares it
numerically without checking it is a number. When the command fails, the
comparison errors and the shell reads the non-zero status as *false*, so
the check is skipped and the script goes on to print `instructions OK`.

A check that silently stops existing is worse than no check: the build
is green and the reason is invisible.

Three places, all pre-existing:

- `agentsbytes` and `claudebytes` — `wc -c` at lines 59-60, compared at
  63 and 131
- `claudelines` — `grep -cv` at 135, compared at 136

Reproduced with `grep` unavailable:

```
instructions.sh: 135: grep: not found
instructions.sh: 136: [: Illegal number:
instructions OK (CLAUDE.md 174 bytes, AGENTS.md 23614 bytes)
```

Exit 0. The line-count check did not run and nothing said so.

## Why it matters here specifically

This is the file that guards every other instruction rule — the one that
keeps `CLAUDE.md` a pointer and `AGENTS.md` present. It is the last
place that should fail open.

## Already fixed in one place, and unprotected

The same shape was found and fixed for the finding-standard count added
for #97: a `case '' | *[!0-9]*` guard now reports "this check did not
run" instead of falling through. The three above were left alone as
out-of-slice.

Note what is *not* covered: deleting that guard and restoring the bare
comparison reopens the hole and all 11 tests still pass. The fix has no
regression test, because testing it needs a fake `awk`/`wc`/`grep` on
`PATH` — which is how it was verified, but from a harness built outside
the repository rather than from anything in the tree.

## Suggested approach

One helper, used by all four sites, that takes the captured value and
the check's name and fails with "this check did not run" when the value
is not a number. Then decide whether a harness that shadows `awk`, `wc`
and `grep` is worth carrying in `tests/` to keep the guards honest —
that is the part that would actually stop this returning.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] No check in `tests/instructions.sh` can be skipped by a failing
      command without the script failing.
- [ ] Proven able to fail, per AGENTS.md step 4 — a shadowed binary is
      how the existing guard was proven.

Found by `verifier` while verifying #97, which fixed the fourth
instance. Follow the workflow in [AGENTS.md](../blob/main/AGENTS.md).
EOF
)"

## Verdict

**Request changes** — two should-fixes. Reviewed state: branch `docs/align-finding-standards` at `753556c` (identical to `main`; the entire change is unstaged) plus the two modified files `AGENTS.md` and `tests/instructions.sh`. No staged or untracked content. Nothing else pending.

I verified all three claims you asked about, and both of them hold along with the third:

- **"steps 6, 7 and 8 each condition theirs on a change"** — true. `AGENTS.md:208` ("If fixing one changes what the game shows a player"), `:221` ("If a verifier finding requires a code change"), `:228` ("If review findings cause changes").
- **"step 11 forbids repeating `code-review` over an unchanged worktree"** — true. `AGENTS.md:301-302`, "Do not repeat code review when the already-reviewed diff and worktree remain unchanged."
- **"step 8 already carries `ui-review` facts into `code-review`"** — true. `AGENTS.md:232-234`.

Also verified: the counted phrase appears exactly 4 times (steps 6, 7, 8 and the section), it wraps mid-phrase in exactly 2 of the 4 as the comment claims, it holds no regex metacharacter, and both new checks demonstrably fail — rewording step 7 back to "Address every actionable finding" gives `3 times, expected 4`, renaming the heading trips the second, and running with `awk` off `PATH` trips the non-number guard instead of printing `instructions OK`. The test is registered in `CMakeLists.txt:122-125`. The #65 correction is posted and its arithmetic is right.

## Findings

### should-fix — `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/AGENTS.md:402-403` vs `:284`

The section now explicitly sanctions committing over a `code-review` finding that was resolved rather than fixed ("there is no next pass"), while step 10 still leads with **"Commit after approval."**

Failure scenario, and it is the one #97 exists to prevent: an agent judges a `code-review` finding wrong, resolves it explicitly, and then reads step 10 and has no approve verdict in hand. It either re-invokes `code-review` over an unchanged worktree — which step 11 forbids and which burns a pass — or gives up and fixes the finding it believes is wrong, which is exactly the "reasoned disagreement turns into an unnecessary fix" outcome the issue names. Before this diff, step 8's vague "Address" made step 10's lead roughly true; making the route explicit is what puts the two in tension.

Suggested fix: one clause, in whichever place you prefer. Either step 10 — "Commit only after verification and code review are complete, with every finding fixed or explicitly resolved" — or a half-sentence in the new paragraph saying that a finding resolved explicitly satisfies step 10 without a fresh approval. Step 10's body already reads "complete" rather than "approved", so this is a lead-in that no longer matches, not a rewrite.

### should-fix — `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/instructions.sh:77-82`, with `:112-113`

This answers your third question directly: **yes, there is such a state, and it is a one-place edit.** The comment discloses only the coordinated edit ("reworded a step and added the phrase somewhere else"), and claims the pair "catches the one-place regression". It does not catch this one.

Step 6's clause at `AGENTS.md:206-207` — `the standard that "Answering a finding" below sets for all three passes` — is the *only* reference from the numbered steps to the section. Delete just that clause and leave the counted phrase in place: the count stays 4, the heading is still there, and `instructions.sh` prints `instructions OK`. I ran it. The section is then orphaned, and a reader of steps 7 or 8 has nothing telling them where a resolution is recorded — #97's second acceptance criterion, silently lost. The heading check's own message asserts "step 6 points at it by name", which is the thing nothing verifies.

Suggested fix, cheapest first: `grep -q '"Answering a finding"' "$AGENTS"` as a third check — the quoted form appears only in step 6's pointer, the heading is unquoted, so it separates cleanly and needs no counted literal (nothing for #65 to inherit). Failing that, amend the comment at `:77-82` so the disclosed gap covers the pointer as well as the coordinated edit, and drop the "step 6 points at it by name" assertion from the message at `:113`.

### nit — process disclosure

Your invocation covered `verifier` thoroughly but made no claim either way about `ui-review`. Per step 8 the skip has to be stated, not left out. I am not treating it as a blocker because the diff plainly cannot reach the player — prose in `AGENTS.md` and a shell script that nothing compiles, no `sst` source, no CMake feature flags, and `AGENTS.md:328` names this file as one that "usually give[s] it nothing to read". State the skip and the reason in the commit and the pull request body anyway, since those are the record.

## Reads well, no change asked

The four paragraphs are a rule, not an essay — each does one job (which two ways exist, what fixing is, what resolving is, where it goes, what does not count), and I would not trim further. The scoping against step 9 at `:409-413` is now correct in both directions. The `Where it goes` paragraph is the densest and reads slightly against its own opening (it "depends", then "Either way it goes in the pull request body"), but the two destinations are genuinely different and I could not shorten it without losing one.

## Verdict

**Request changes** — two should-fixes. Reviewed state: branch `docs/align-finding-standards` at `753556c` (identical to `main`; the entire change is unstaged) plus the two modified files `AGENTS.md` and `tests/instructions.sh`. No staged or untracked content. Nothing else pending.

I verified all three claims you asked about, and both of them hold along with the third:

- **"steps 6, 7 and 8 each condition theirs on a change"** — true. `AGENTS.md:208` ("If fixing one changes what the game shows a player"), `:221` ("If a verifier finding requires a code change"), `:228` ("If review findings cause changes").
- **"step 11 forbids repeating `code-review` over an unchanged worktree"** — true. `AGENTS.md:301-302`, "Do not repeat code review when the already-reviewed diff and worktree remain unchanged."
- **"step 8 already carries `ui-review` facts into `code-review`"** — true. `AGENTS.md:232-234`.

Also verified: the counted phrase appears exactly 4 times (steps 6, 7, 8 and the section), it wraps mid-phrase in exactly 2 of the 4 as the comment claims, it holds no regex metacharacter, and both new checks demonstrably fail — rewording step 7 back to "Address every actionable finding" gives `3 times, expected 4`, renaming the heading trips the second, and running with `awk` off `PATH` trips the non-number guard instead of printing `instructions OK`. The test is registered in `CMakeLists.txt:122-125`. The #65 correction is posted and its arithmetic is right.

## Findings

### should-fix — `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/AGENTS.md:402-403` vs `:284`

The section now explicitly sanctions committing over a `code-review` finding that was resolved rather than fixed ("there is no next pass"), while step 10 still leads with **"Commit after approval."**

Failure scenario, and it is the one #97 exists to prevent: an agent judges a `code-review` finding wrong, resolves it explicitly, and then reads step 10 and has no approve verdict in hand. It either re-invokes `code-review` over an unchanged worktree — which step 11 forbids and which burns a pass — or gives up and fixes the finding it believes is wrong, which is exactly the "reasoned disagreement turns into an unnecessary fix" outcome the issue names. Before this diff, step 8's vague "Address" made step 10's lead roughly true; making the route explicit is what puts the two in tension.

Suggested fix: one clause, in whichever place you prefer. Either step 10 — "Commit only after verification and code review are complete, with every finding fixed or explicitly resolved" — or a half-sentence in the new paragraph saying that a finding resolved explicitly satisfies step 10 without a fresh approval. Step 10's body already reads "complete" rather than "approved", so this is a lead-in that no longer matches, not a rewrite.

### should-fix — `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/instructions.sh:77-82`, with `:112-113`

This answers your third question directly: **yes, there is such a state, and it is a one-place edit.** The comment discloses only the coordinated edit ("reworded a step and added the phrase somewhere else"), and claims the pair "catches the one-place regression". It does not catch this one.

Delete just that clause and leave the counted phrase in place: the count stays 4, the heading is still there, and `instructions.sh` prints `instructions OK`. I ran it. The section is then orphaned, and a reader of steps 7 or 8 has nothing telling them where a resolution is recorded — #97's second acceptance criterion, silently lost. The heading check's own message asserts "step 6 points at it by name", which is the thing nothing verifies.

Suggested fix, cheapest first: `grep -q '"Answering a finding"' "$AGENTS"` as a third check — the quoted form appears only in step 6's pointer, the heading is unquoted, so it separates cleanly and needs no counted literal (nothing for #65 to inherit). Failing that, amend the comment at `:77-82` so the disclosed gap covers the pointer as well as the coordinated edit, and drop the "step 6 points at it by name" assertion from the message at `:113`.

### nit — process disclosure

Your invocation covered `verifier` thoroughly but made no claim either way about `ui-review`. Per step 8 the skip has to be stated, not left out. I am not treating it as a blocker because the diff plainly cannot reach the player — prose in `AGENTS.md` and a shell script that nothing compiles, no `sst` source, no CMake feature flags, and `AGENTS.md:328` names this file as one that "usually give[s] it nothing to read". State the skip and the reason in the commit and the pull request body anyway, since those are the record.

## Reads well, no change asked

The four paragraphs are a rule, not an essay — each does one job (which two ways exist, what fixing is, what resolving is, where it goes, what does not count), and I would not trim further. The scoping against step 9 at `:409-413` is now correct in both directions. The `Where it goes` paragraph is the densest and reads slightly against its own opening (it "depends", then "Either way it goes in the pull request body"), but the two destinations are genuinely different and I could not shorten it without losing one.

#!/bin/sh
# Checks that AGENTS.md stays the single source of truth for project
# instructions, and that CLAUDE.md stays a pointer to it.
#
# Rules drift into CLAUDE.md easily and silently: Claude Code's `#`
# shortcut appends there, `/init` rewrites the file wholesale, and
# tools that target CLAUDE.md by name edit it directly. None of them
# know AGENTS.md exists. Without a check, the result is two sources of
# truth that slowly disagree.
#
# The AGENTS.md checks matter just as much: CLAUDE.md pulls it in with
# an `@AGENTS.md` import, and if that file is renamed, emptied, or
# deleted the import resolves to nothing -- no error, no warning, just
# an agent session with no rules at all.
#
# Usage: instructions.sh /path/to/repo/root

set -u

ROOT="${1:-.}"
while [ "${ROOT%/}" != "$ROOT" ] && [ "$ROOT" != "/" ]; do
	ROOT="${ROOT%/}"
done
CLAUDE="$ROOT/CLAUDE.md"
AGENTS="$ROOT/AGENTS.md"

# The pointer needs a title, a sentence or two, and the import. Kept
# tight on purpose: headroom here is room for a rule to hide by being
# folded into an existing line rather than added as a new one, which
# the line budget below cannot see. A very short phrase can still fit;
# that one is left to review.
MAXBYTES=220
# CLAUDE.md is meant to be frozen, so this is the exact number of
# non-blank lines it has today, not a generous budget: a rule slipped in
# as plain prose adds a line and nothing else would. Changing the
# pointer's wording means changing this number on purpose. The prose is
# wrapped at 72 columns to match the rest of the repo -- rewrapping it
# much narrower will need a third line and trip this.
MAXLINES=4
# Enough that a gutted or stub AGENTS.md fails, well under its real size.
MINAGENTS=2000

fails=0
fail() {
	printf 'FAIL: %s\n' "$1" >&2
	fails=$((fails + 1))
}

if [ ! -f "$AGENTS" ]; then
	fail "AGENTS.md is missing -- CLAUDE.md's @AGENTS.md import would silently resolve to nothing"
fi
if [ ! -f "$CLAUDE" ]; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md is missing -- Claude Code sessions would load no project rules"
fi
if [ "$fails" -ne 0 ]; then
	exit 1
fi

agentsbytes=$(wc -c < "$AGENTS" | tr -d ' ')
claudebytes=$(wc -c < "$CLAUDE" | tr -d ' ')

# AGENTS.md holds the real content.
if [ "$agentsbytes" -lt "$MINAGENTS" ]; then
	fail "AGENTS.md is only $agentsbytes bytes; expected at least $MINAGENTS -- has its content been moved or lost?"
fi
if ! grep -q '^## Development workflow' "$AGENTS"; then
	fail "AGENTS.md has no '## Development workflow' section -- the workflow every agent follows should live there"
fi

# Steps 6, 7 and 8 hold their review passes to one standard, and say it
# in one form of words so a reader can see that they agree. They did not
# always: two said "address every actionable finding" and the middle one
# said "fix or explicitly resolve", while the first claimed to be
# stating the same rule "as with the two steps below". Nobody noticed
# until a reviewer read all three together.
#
# Counted, not located: hard-coding line numbers would break on every
# edit above them, and nothing here can tell which step a match fell in.
# So this catches the one-place regression -- a step reworded on its own
# -- and not a coordinated edit that reworded a step and added the
# phrase somewhere else to keep the total at four. Issue #65 is the
# check that would know one step from another.
#
# Counted over the file with its line breaks flattened, because the
# phrase wraps mid-sentence in two of the four places it appears: a
# check a rewrap can break is a check that gets deleted the first time
# someone rewraps. The phrase holds no regex metacharacter, so passing
# it to awk as a pattern matches it literally; one added later would
# quietly turn this into something else.
STANDARD='actionable finding, or resolve it explicitly'
# Three steps state it and one section defines it. Stating it a fifth
# time on purpose means changing this number on purpose.
STANDARDS=4
standards=$(awk -v want="$STANDARD" '
	{ s = s " " $0 }
	END { gsub(/[ \t]+/, " ", s); print gsub(want, "&", s) }' "$AGENTS")
# A non-number means awk did not run -- unsupported construct, missing
# binary, anything. Compared directly against STANDARDS that is not a
# failure but a silent pass: the test errors "Illegal number", `if`
# reads the non-zero status as false, and the script goes on to print
# "instructions OK". A check that stops existing has to say so.
case "$standards" in
'' | *[!0-9]*)
	fail "could not count the finding standard in AGENTS.md -- awk printed '$standards' instead of a number, so this check did not run"
	;;
*)
	if [ "$standards" -ne "$STANDARDS" ]; then
		fail "AGENTS.md states the finding standard $standards times, expected $STANDARDS -- steps 6, 7 and 8 each state it and 'Answering a finding' defines it. A step reworded on its own no longer visibly agrees with the others; if you added a statement of it on purpose, update STANDARDS in this script"
	fi
	;;
esac
if ! grep -q '^### Answering a finding' "$AGENTS"; then
	fail "AGENTS.md has no '### Answering a finding' section -- step 6 points at it by name, and it is where the standard the three steps state is defined"
fi

# CLAUDE.md points at it and holds nothing else.
if ! grep -q '^@AGENTS\.md[[:space:]]*$' "$CLAUDE"; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md has no '@AGENTS.md' import line -- Claude Code would not load the shared rules"
fi
# Blank out the one allowed import and see if any other remains. An
# import works mid-line too, so matching only at the start of a line
# would miss `... see @RULES.md:` -- four lines, small, and a second
# source of truth in every session. Only whole tokens are blanked, or
# `@AGENTS.md.bak` would be read as the allowed import plus nothing --
# and since `.` has to count as part of a token for that, sentence
# punctuation after the import is absorbed too.
if sed -E 's#@AGENTS\.md([.,;:!?]?)([^A-Za-z0-9._/-]|$)#\1\2#g' "$CLAUDE" \
		| grep -q '@[A-Za-z0-9._/-]'; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md imports a file other than AGENTS.md -- rules should reach agents through AGENTS.md alone"
fi
if [ "$claudebytes" -gt "$MAXBYTES" ]; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md is $claudebytes bytes, over the $MAXBYTES limit -- rules belong in AGENTS.md, not here"
fi

claudelines=$(grep -cv '^[[:space:]]*$' "$CLAUDE")
if [ "$claudelines" -gt "$MAXLINES" ]; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md has $claudelines non-blank lines, expected at most $MAXLINES -- if you added a rule, move it to AGENTS.md; if you reworded the pointer, update MAXLINES in this script"
fi

# Rules arrive as list items or new sections. The pointer needs neither,
# so their presence below the title means content landed in the wrong file.
if tail -n +2 "$CLAUDE" | grep -qE '^[[:space:]]*(#|[-*+][[:space:]]|[0-9]+\.[[:space:]])'; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md contains headings or list items below the title -- move that content to AGENTS.md"
fi

# Claude Code also loads CLAUDE.md files from subdirectories (when working
# under them) and from .claude/. Any of those is a second shared source of
# truth, so only the root pointer may exist. A personal, unshared
# CLAUDE.local.md at the root is deliberately left alone -- .gitignore
# keeps it from becoming a shared one.
#
# Matched case-insensitively: macOS filesystems are case-insensitive by
# default, so a lone claude.md there would load like the real thing.
# The prune list mirrors .gitignore's build trees rather than any
# directory merely starting with "build".
extra=$(find "$ROOT" \( -name .git -o -name build -o -name 'build-*' \) -prune -o \
	-iname 'CLAUDE*.md' \
	! -ipath "$ROOT/CLAUDE.md" \
	! -ipath "$ROOT/CLAUDE.local.md" \
	-print 2>/dev/null)
if [ -n "$extra" ]; then
	fail "these files also carry instructions; fold them into AGENTS.md:"
	echo "$extra" | sed 's/^/         /' >&2
fi

if [ "$fails" -ne 0 ]; then
	printf '\n%d check(s) failed.\n' "$fails" >&2
	printf 'AGENTS.md is the source of truth for every coding agent; CLAUDE.md only imports it.\n' >&2
	printf 'Put project rules in AGENTS.md and leave CLAUDE.md as the pointer.\n' >&2
	exit 1
fi

printf 'instructions OK (CLAUDE.md %s bytes, AGENTS.md %s bytes)\n' "$claudebytes" "$agentsbytes"

Both applied. Please re-read `AGENTS.md` and `tests/instructions.sh` from the repository and give a verdict.

**1. Step 10 versus explicit resolution.** You were right that making the route explicit is what put them in tension — "Address" was vague enough to paper over it. Step 10 now reads:

> **Commit once the passes are answered.** Commit only after verification and code review are complete, with every finding fixed or explicitly resolved — a finding resolved rather than fixed needs no fresh approval, which is why this does not say "after approval".

I changed the bold lead as well as the body. Your suggestion kept "Commit after approval" and added the clause, but the lead is the part an agent skimming a twelve-step list actually reads, and leaving it saying "approval" while the body says otherwise recreates the defect one line up. Tell me if you think the lead should have stayed — it is the one place I went further than you asked.

**2. The one-place edit that defeated both checks.** Confirmed and fixed. There is now a third check, `grep -q '"Answering a finding"'`, on your reasoning that the quoted form appears only in step 6's pointer while the heading is unquoted — I verified that separation holds today: one match at line 207, the heading at 384 unquoted, nothing else.

Proven rather than asserted: I built the mutant you described, deleting only step 6's pointer clause and leaving the counted phrase in place, in a copy outside the repository. docs: hold the three review passes to one standard

Steps 6, 7 and 8 stated two standards while step 6 asserted they were
one. Six and eight said "Address every actionable finding"; seven said
"Fix or explicitly resolve"; and six said its version applied "as with
the two steps below". A fourth phrasing sat in step 9, which called a
finding "resolved" without either of the other steps introducing that
as something a finding could be. So the file claimed the three passes
were held to the same standard in the same sentence that gave one of
them a different one -- worse than an inconsistency a reader might miss,
because a reader who noticed had been told the difference did not
matter.

The three steps now use one form of words, and a new section says what
the second half of it means. Resolving explicitly is for the finding you
judge wrong, or right about something the change is not: say what you
think is true instead, to the next pass that runs anyway, and in the
pull request body. Not to the pass that raised it -- a resolution alters
no code, so it triggers no rerun, and step 11 forbids repeating
code-review over an unchanged worktree. That route was in the first
draft and code-review found it named a moment the workflow does not
provide.

Step 10 led with "Commit after approval", which was roughly true while
"Address" was vague enough to cover both dispositions. Making the route
explicit is what put the two in tension, so it now leads with what it
means: commit once the passes are answered, a finding resolved rather
than fixed needing no fresh approval.

tests/instructions.sh holds the standard to exactly four statements --
three steps and the definition -- and requires both the section and the
pointer to it. The count is taken over the file with its line breaks
flattened, because the phrase wraps mid-sentence in two of the four
places; a check a rewrap can break is a check that gets deleted the
first time someone rewraps.

Three of the four checks in that file were shown to fail open before
this: a command that errors leaves a non-number, the numeric comparison
errors in turn, and the shell reads that non-zero status as false, so
the check is skipped and the script still prints "instructions OK".
The one added here is guarded and says when it did not run. The three
that predate it are #98.

Each new check was proven by breaking what it claims to cover, in
copies outside the repository: step 8 reworded back to "Address", the
section renamed, a fifth statement added, awk shadowed by a stub that
exits, and step 6's pointer deleted on its own -- which the first two
checks passed and the third catches.

ui-review did not run and is not owed: prose and a shell script,
nothing compiled, no sst source, no CMake feature flag, no sst.doc.

Also filed: #98 above, and corrections to #65 -- one recording what the
count cannot see, and one withdrawing a claim of mine that a CRLF
conversion could not break it. It can; the count drops from four to two,
because the flattening collapses spaces and tabs and a carriage return
is neither.

Closes #97

#!/bin/sh
# Checks that AGENTS.md stays the single source of truth for project
# instructions, and that CLAUDE.md stays a pointer to it.
#
# Rules drift into CLAUDE.md easily and silently: Claude Code's `#`
# shortcut appends there, `/init` rewrites the file wholesale, and
# tools that target CLAUDE.md by name edit it directly. None of them
# know AGENTS.md exists. Without a check, the result is two sources of
# truth that slowly disagree.
#
# The AGENTS.md checks matter just as much: CLAUDE.md pulls it in with
# an `@AGENTS.md` import, and if that file is renamed, emptied, or
# deleted the import resolves to nothing -- no error, no warning, just
# an agent session with no rules at all.
#
# Usage: instructions.sh /path/to/repo/root

set -u

ROOT="${1:-.}"
while [ "${ROOT%/}" != "$ROOT" ] && [ "$ROOT" != "/" ]; do
	ROOT="${ROOT%/}"
done
CLAUDE="$ROOT/CLAUDE.md"
AGENTS="$ROOT/AGENTS.md"

# The pointer needs a title, a sentence or two, and the import. Kept
# tight on purpose: headroom here is room for a rule to hide by being
# folded into an existing line rather than added as a new one, which
# the line budget below cannot see. A very short phrase can still fit;
# that one is left to review.
MAXBYTES=220
# CLAUDE.md is meant to be frozen, so this is the exact number of
# non-blank lines it has today, not a generous budget: a rule slipped in
# as plain prose adds a line and nothing else would. Changing the
# pointer's wording means changing this number on purpose. The prose is
# wrapped at 72 columns to match the rest of the repo -- rewrapping it
# much narrower will need a third line and trip this.
MAXLINES=4
# Enough that a gutted or stub AGENTS.md fails, well under its real size.
MINAGENTS=2000

fails=0
fail() {
	printf 'FAIL: %s\n' "$1" >&2
	fails=$((fails + 1))
}

if [ ! -f "$AGENTS" ]; then
	fail "AGENTS.md is missing -- CLAUDE.md's @AGENTS.md import would silently resolve to nothing"
fi
if [ ! -f "$CLAUDE" ]; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md is missing -- Claude Code sessions would load no project rules"
fi
if [ "$fails" -ne 0 ]; then
	exit 1
fi

agentsbytes=$(wc -c < "$AGENTS" | tr -d ' ')
claudebytes=$(wc -c < "$CLAUDE" | tr -d ' ')

# AGENTS.md holds the real content.
if [ "$agentsbytes" -lt "$MINAGENTS" ]; then
	fail "AGENTS.md is only $agentsbytes bytes; expected at least $MINAGENTS -- has its content been moved or lost?"
fi
if ! grep -q '^## Development workflow' "$AGENTS"; then

approval", which was roughly true only while "Address" was vague enough

Three of my own claims were the same defect this change removes — prose
asserting an agreement the numbered steps do not have:

- "step 11 forbids repeating **a pass**", where step 11 names

it flattens line breaks. `\r` is neither space nor tab, so it survives —

exactly four times (three steps, one definition), the section must

#
# Rules drift into CLAUDE.md easily and silently: Claude Code's `#`
# shortcut appends there, `/init` rewrites the file wholesale, and
# tools that target CLAUDE.md by name edit it directly. None of them
# know AGENTS.md exists. Without a check, the result is two sources of
# truth that slowly disagree.
#
# The AGENTS.md checks matter just as much: CLAUDE.md pulls it in with
# an `@AGENTS.md` import, and if that file is renamed, emptied, or
# deleted the import resolves to nothing -- no error, no warning, just
# an agent session with no rules at all.
#
# Usage: instructions.sh /path/to/repo/root

set -u

ROOT="${1:-.}"
while [ "${ROOT%/}" != "$ROOT" ] && [ "$ROOT" != "/" ]; do
	ROOT="${ROOT%/}"
done
CLAUDE="$ROOT/CLAUDE.md"
AGENTS="$ROOT/AGENTS.md"

# The pointer needs a title, a sentence or two, and the import. Kept
# tight on purpose: headroom here is room for a rule to hide by being
# folded into an existing line rather than added as a new one, which
# the line budget below cannot see. A very short phrase can still fit;
# that one is left to review.
MAXBYTES=220
# CLAUDE.md is meant to be frozen, so this is the exact number of
# non-blank lines it has today, not a generous budget: a rule slipped in
# as plain prose adds a line and nothing else would. Changing the
# pointer's wording means changing this number on purpose. The prose is
# wrapped at 72 columns to match the rest of the repo -- rewrapping it
# much narrower will need a third line and trip this.
MAXLINES=4
# Enough that a gutted or stub AGENTS.md fails, well under its real size.
MINAGENTS=2000

fails=0
fail() {
	printf 'FAIL: %s\n' "$1" >&2
	fails=$((fails + 1))
}

if [ ! -f "$AGENTS" ]; then
	fail "AGENTS.md is missing -- CLAUDE.md's @AGENTS.md import would silently resolve to nothing"
fi
if [ ! -f "$CLAUDE" ]; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md is missing -- Claude Code sessions would load no project rules"
fi
if [ "$fails" -ne 0 ]; then
	exit 1
fi

agentsbytes=$(wc -c < "$AGENTS" | tr -d ' ')
claudebytes=$(wc -c < "$CLAUDE" | tr -d ' ')

# AGENTS.md holds the real content.
if [ "$agentsbytes" -lt "$MINAGENTS" ]; then
	fail "AGENTS.md is only $agentsbytes bytes; expected at least $MINAGENTS -- has its content been moved or lost?"
fi
if ! grep -q '^## Development workflow' "$AGENTS"; then
	fail "AGENTS.md has no '## Development workflow' section -- the workflow every agent follows should live there"
fi

# Steps 6, 7 and 8 hold their review passes to one standard, and say it
# in one form of words so a reader can see that they agree. They did not
# always: two said "address every actionable finding" and the middle one
# said "fix or explicitly resolve", while the first claimed to be
# stating the same rule "as with the two steps below". Nobody noticed
# until a reviewer read all three together.
#
# Counted, not located: hard-coding line numbers would break on every
# edit above them, and nothing here can tell which step a match fell in.
# So this catches the one-place regression -- a step reworded on its own
# -- and not a coordinated edit that reworded a step and added the
# phrase somewhere else to keep the total at four. Issue #65 is the
# check that would know one step from another.
#
# Counted over the file with its line breaks flattened, because the
# phrase wraps mid-sentence in two of the four places it appears: a
# check a rewrap can break is a check that gets deleted the first time
# someone rewraps. The phrase holds no regex metacharacter, so passing
# it to awk as a pattern matches it literally; one added later would
# quietly turn this into something else.
STANDARD='actionable finding, or resolve it explicitly'
# Three steps state it and one section defines it. Stating it a fifth
# time on purpose means changing this number on purpose.
STANDARDS=4
standards=$(awk -v want="$STANDARD" '
	{ s = s " " $0 }
	END { gsub(/[ \t]+/, " ", s); print gsub(want, "&", s) }' "$AGENTS")
# A non-number means awk did not run -- unsupported construct, missing
# binary, anything. Compared directly against STANDARDS that is not a
# failure but a silent pass: the test errors "Illegal number", `if`
# reads the non-zero status as false, and the script goes on to print
# "instructions OK". A check that stops existing has to say so.
case "$standards" in
'' | *[!0-9]*)
	fail "could not count the finding standard in AGENTS.md -- awk printed '$standards' instead of a number, so this check did not run"
	;;
*)
	if [ "$standards" -ne "$STANDARDS" ]; then
		fail "AGENTS.md states the finding standard $standards times, expected $STANDARDS -- steps 6, 7 and 8 each state it and 'Answering a finding' defines it. A step reworded on its own no longer visibly agrees with the others; if you added a statement of it on purpose, update STANDARDS in this script"
	fi
	;;
esac
SECTION='Answering a finding'
if ! grep -q "^### $SECTION" "$AGENTS"; then
	fail "AGENTS.md has no '### $SECTION' section -- step 6 points at it by name, and it is where the standard the three steps state is defined"
fi
# And the pointer to it, which is the one thing tying the numbered steps
# to the definition. Delete just that clause and the count above still
# reads 4 and the heading is still there: the section goes on existing
# with nothing sending a reader to it, which loses the half of #97 that
# asked where a disagreement is recorded. Matched in quotes because the
# heading itself is unquoted, so this finds the reference and not the
# thing referred to.
if ! grep -q "\"$SECTION\"" "$AGENTS"; then
	fail "nothing in AGENTS.md refers to \"$SECTION\" -- the section defines the standard steps 6, 7 and 8 state, and nothing now sends a reader to it"
fi

# CLAUDE.md points at it and holds nothing else.
if ! grep -q '^@AGENTS\.md[[:space:]]*$' "$CLAUDE"; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md has no '@AGENTS.md' import line -- Claude Code would not load the shared rules"
fi
# Blank out the one allowed import and see if any other remains. An
# import works mid-line too, so matching only at the start of a line
# would miss `... see @RULES.md:` -- four lines, small, and a second
# source of truth in every session. Only whole tokens are blanked, or
# `@AGENTS.md.bak` would be read as the allowed import plus nothing --
# and since `.` has to count as part of a token for that, sentence
# punctuation after the import is absorbed too.
if sed -E 's#@AGENTS\.md([.,;:!?]?)([^A-Za-z0-9._/-]|$)#\1\2#g' "$CLAUDE" \
		| grep -q '@[A-Za-z0-9._/-]'; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md imports a file other than AGENTS.md -- rules should reach agents through AGENTS.md alone"
fi
if [ "$claudebytes" -gt "$MAXBYTES" ]; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md is $claudebytes bytes, over the $MAXBYTES limit -- rules belong in AGENTS.md, not here"
fi

claudelines=$(grep -cv '^[[:space:]]*$' "$CLAUDE")
if [ "$claudelines" -gt "$MAXLINES" ]; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md has $claudelines non-blank lines, expected at most $MAXLINES -- if you added a rule, move it to AGENTS.md; if you reworded the pointer, update MAXLINES in this script"
fi

# Rules arrive as list items or new sections. The pointer needs neither,
# so their presence below the title means content landed in the wrong file.
if tail -n +2 "$CLAUDE" | grep -qE '^[[:space:]]*(#|[-*+][[:space:]]|[0-9]+\.[[:space:]])'; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md contains headings or list items below the title -- move that content to AGENTS.md"
fi

# Claude Code also loads CLAUDE.md files from subdirectories (when working
# under them) and from .claude/. Any of those is a second shared source of
# truth, so only the root pointer may exist. A personal, unshared
# CLAUDE.local.md at the root is deliberately left alone -- .gitignore
# keeps it from becoming a shared one.
#
# Matched case-insensitively: macOS filesystems are case-insensitive by
# default, so a lone claude.md there would load like the real thing.
# The prune list mirrors .gitignore's build trees rather than any
# directory merely starting with "build".
extra=$(find "$ROOT" \( -name .git -o -name build -o -name 'build-*' \) -prune -o \
	-iname 'CLAUDE*.md' \
	! -ipath "$ROOT/CLAUDE.md" \
	! -ipath "$ROOT/CLAUDE.local.md" \
	-print 2>/dev/null)
if [ -n "$extra" ]; then
	fail "these files also carry instructions; fold them into AGENTS.md:"
	echo "$extra" | sed 's/^/         /' >&2
fi

if [ "$fails" -ne 0 ]; then
	printf '\n%d check(s) failed.\n' "$fails" >&2
	printf 'AGENTS.md is the source of truth for every coding agent; CLAUDE.md only imports it.\n' >&2
	printf 'Put project rules in AGENTS.md and leave CLAUDE.md as the pointer.\n' >&2
	exit 1
fi

printf 'instructions OK (CLAUDE.md %s bytes, AGENTS.md %s bytes)\n' "$claudebytes" "$agentsbytes"

## Verdict: pass

Both fixes hold. The reported hole is closed, the citation checks out against the file on disk, and everything else you asked me to confirm still holds. Two low-severity observations below, neither blocking.

---

## 1. The awk guard (`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/instructions.sh:104-119`)

**The hole is real and is closed.** Same stub (`printf "4\n"; exit 17`), same reworded-step-8 fixture, both scripts:

```
old.sh (ac5ebf2):  instructions OK (CLAUDE.md 174 bytes, AGENTS.md 23984 bytes)   rc=0
new.sh:            FAIL: could not count the finding standard in AGENTS.md --
                   awk exited non-zero, so this check did not run whatever it printed   rc=1
```

**Exit-status half fires on its own** (each produced exactly one FAIL, rc=1): `printf 4; exit 17`; `exit 127`; `awk` absent from `PATH` entirely (`awk: not found`); awk killed by SIGTERM *after* printing `4`; awk failing on an unreadable `AGENTS.md`; and — a case neither of us tried — an **exported bash function** shadowing `awk` (`export -f awk`), which bypasses `PATH` and still gets caught.

**Non-number half fires on its own** (awk exits 0): empty output, `banana`, `" 4 "` (leading/trailing spaces), `4\n4`, `-4`, `4\r`. All rc=1 with the `printed '...'` message.

**Neither masks the other.** With both wrong (`banana` + exit 17) only the exit-status message prints — still rc=1, never a pass. There is no combination where one branch's failure becomes a green. The count check remains bidirectional: reworded step 8 → "states the finding standard 3 times"; a fifth instance appended → "5 times".

**Status propagation — the part you were least sure of.** I tested `if ! v=$(cmd)` directly with five shapes (nonzero after output, zero, 127, death by signal, command-not-found) in **dash, bash 5.3, bash --posix, busybox ash**: correct in all four. POSIX XCU 2.9.1 mandates it ("If there is no command name, but the command contained a command substitution, the command shall complete with the exit status of the last command substitution"). Legitimate runs pass everywhere: real repo + both fixtures × those four shells × mawk 1.3.4 and busybox awk × locales `C`, `C.UTF-8`, `en_US.UTF-8`, `tr_TR.UTF-8`, `POSIX` (the locale sweep is for the `*[!0-9]*` bracket expression), plus `ROOT` containing a space, trailing-slash and triple-slash `ROOT`, and an `AGENTS.md` with no trailing newline. 10/10 direct runs and 5/5 `ctest -R instructions` runs — deterministic, no flakes.

**Cases neither of us tried, with results:** awk killed by a signal after a valid count (caught); awk writing warnings to stderr and exiting 0 (passes, correctly); `" 4 "`, `4\r`, `-4`, two-line output (all caught); exported shell function shadowing awk (caught); `AGENTS.md` converted to CRLF → fails **loudly** with count 2, so a Windows/autocrlf checkout is a red test, not a silent pass; awk that hangs → the script hangs and only `set_tests_properties(instructions PROPERTIES TIMEOUT 30)` stops it (adequate, pre-existing).

**Observation A — residual silent pass, negligible but the comment overstates.** A digits-only value too large for shell arithmetic still passes the `case` and then dies non-fatally in `[`:

```
$ PATH=stub-bignum:$PATH dash new.sh good     # stub prints 99999999999999999999, exit 0
new.sh: 114: [: Illegal number: 99999999999999999999
instructions OK (...)   rc=0
```

Same under bash. This is exactly the shape the new comment describes, via the one input `*[!0-9]*` accepts but `[ -ne ]` cannot parse. Unreachable from a real awk (a `gsub` count cannot exceed file size), so I would not act on it — but the comment's claim that "both halves of awk's answer are checked" is not quite the whole truth.

**Observation B — pre-existing, outside the diff, step 9 material.** The same unchecked-status shape survives 45 lines earlier: `agentsbytes=$(wc -c < "$AGENTS" | tr -d ' ')` at line 59. With `AGENTS.md` unreadable, line 59 errors, line 63 prints `[: Illegal number: ` and the `MINAGENTS` check silently does not run. The run still exited 1 because other checks failed for their own reasons, but that check itself was a no-op. Worth filing; not this slice's job.

---

## 2. `AGENTS.md` — the steps 3 and 9 citation

**The citation is correct.** Read from `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/AGENTS.md` on disk, not from context. Step boundaries by heading scan: step 3 = lines 109-144, step 9 = 246-283.

- Step 3, lines 131-132: "the pull request body and in the summary of the work, in the summary alone when there is no pull request"
- Step 9, lines 278-280: "in the pull request body and in the summary of the work — in the summary alone when there is no pull request"

Both are the numbered steps named, and both set that fallback. The fourth claim of this shape holds.

**One precision caveat.** Steps 3 and 9 require *both* places when a PR exists (PR body **and** summary), with summary-alone as the fallback. The new sentence reads "Either way it goes in the pull request body — or, where the work ends without one, in the summary of the work, on the same terms steps 3 and 9 already set" — PR body *only* when a PR exists. The fallback clause matches exactly; the with-PR half is looser than what steps 3 and 9 set. "On the same terms" attaches naturally to the fallback, so I would not call it wrong, but it is the one sentence a reader could bounce.

**No contradiction with step 10 or 11.** Step 11 (296-303) says "Rerun `code-review` only if the reviewed state changed" and "Do not repeat code review when the already-reviewed diff and worktree remain unchanged" — the section's characterization is accurate, and adding a record location imposes no rerun. Step 10 (284-287) already says a resolved finding "needs no fresh approval", which a summary-recorded resolution satisfies. Nothing in the workflow requires every change to have a PR — steps 3 and 9 assume otherwise — so the fallback creates no conflict. #!/bin/sh
# Checks that AGENTS.md stays the single source of truth for project
# instructions, and that CLAUDE.md stays a pointer to it.
#
# Rules drift into CLAUDE.md easily and silently: Claude Code's `#`
# shortcut appends there, `/init` rewrites the file wholesale, and
# tools that target CLAUDE.md by name edit it directly. None of them
# know AGENTS.md exists. Without a check, the result is two sources of
# truth that slowly disagree.
#
# The AGENTS.md checks matter just as much: CLAUDE.md pulls it in with
# an `@AGENTS.md` import, and if that file is renamed, emptied, or
# deleted the import resolves to nothing -- no error, no warning, just
# an agent session with no rules at all.
#
# Usage: instructions.sh /path/to/repo/root

set -u

ROOT="${1:-.}"
while [ "${ROOT%/}" != "$ROOT" ] && [ "$ROOT" != "/" ]; do
	ROOT="${ROOT%/}"
done
CLAUDE="$ROOT/CLAUDE.md"
AGENTS="$ROOT/AGENTS.md"

# The pointer needs a title, a sentence or two, and the import. Kept
# tight on purpose: headroom here is room for a rule to hide by being
# folded into an existing line rather than added as a new one, which
# the line budget below cannot see. A very short phrase can still fit;
# that one is left to review.
MAXBYTES=220
# CLAUDE.md is meant to be frozen, so this is the exact number of
# non-blank lines it has today, not a generous budget: a rule slipped in
# as plain prose adds a line and nothing else would. Changing the
# pointer's wording means changing this number on purpose. The prose is
# wrapped at 72 columns to match the rest of the repo -- rewrapping it
# much narrower will need a third line and trip this.
MAXLINES=4
# Enough that a gutted or stub AGENTS.md fails, well under its real size.
MINAGENTS=2000

fails=0
fail() {
	printf 'FAIL: %s\n' "$1" >&2
	fails=$((fails + 1))
}

if [ ! -f "$AGENTS" ]; then
	fail "AGENTS.md is missing -- CLAUDE.md's @AGENTS.md import would silently resolve to nothing"
fi
if [ ! -f "$CLAUDE" ]; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md is missing -- Claude Code sessions would load no project rules"
fi
if [ "$fails" -ne 0 ]; then
	exit 1
fi

agentsbytes=$(wc -c < "$AGENTS" | tr -d ' ')
claudebytes=$(wc -c < "$CLAUDE" | tr -d ' ')

# AGENTS.md holds the real content.
if [ "$agentsbytes" -lt "$MINAGENTS" ]; then
	fail "AGENTS.md is only $agentsbytes bytes; expected at least $MINAGENTS -- has its content been moved or lost?"
fi
if ! grep -q '^## Development workflow' "$AGENTS"; then
	fail "AGENTS.md has no '## Development workflow' section -- the workflow every agent follows should live there"
fi

# Steps 6, 7 and 8 hold their review passes to one standard, and say it
# in one form of words so a reader can see that they agree. They did not
# always: two said "address every actionable finding" and the middle one
# said "fix or explicitly resolve", while the first claimed to be
# stating the same rule "as with the two steps below". Nobody noticed
# until a reviewer read all three together.
#
# Counted, not located: hard-coding line numbers would break on every
# edit above them, and nothing here can tell which step a match fell in.
# So this catches the one-place regression -- a step reworded on its own
# -- and not a coordinated edit that reworded a step and added the
# phrase somewhere else to keep the total at four. Issue #65 is the
# check that would know one step from another.
#
# Counted over the file with its line breaks flattened, because the
# phrase wraps mid-sentence in two of the four places it appears: a
# check a rewrap can break is a check that gets deleted the first time
# someone rewraps. The phrase holds no regex metacharacter, so passing
# it to awk as a pattern matches it literally; one added later would
# quietly turn this into something else.
STANDARD='actionable finding, or resolve it explicitly'
# Three steps state it and one section defines it. Stating it a fifth
# time on purpose means changing this number on purpose.
STANDARDS=4
# Both halves of awk's answer are checked, because either can lie on its
# own. A non-number means it did not run -- unsupported construct,
# missing binary, anything -- and compared directly against STANDARDS
# that is a silent pass rather than a failure: the test errors "Illegal
# number", `if` reads the non-zero status as false, and the script goes
# on to print "instructions OK". A number from a command that then
# failed is the same hole from the other side: a shadowed awk printing
# "4" and exiting 17 satisfied the number check, and did it on a file
# whose step 8 had been reworded back to the old standard -- green,
# with the defect present and the counter never having run.
if ! standards=$(awk -v want="$STANDARD" '
	{ s = s " " $0 }
	END { gsub(/[ \t]+/, " ", s); print gsub(want, "&", s) }' "$AGENTS"); then
	fail "could not count the finding standard in AGENTS.md -- awk exited non-zero, so this check did not run whatever it printed"
else
	case "$standards" in
	'' | *[!0-9]*)
		fail "could not count the finding standard in AGENTS.md -- awk printed '$standards' instead of a number, so this check did not run"
		;;
	*)
		if [ "$standards" -ne "$STANDARDS" ]; then
			fail "AGENTS.md states the finding standard $standards times, expected $STANDARDS -- steps 6, 7 and 8 each state it and 'Answering a finding' defines it. A step reworded on its own no longer visibly agrees with the others; if you added a statement of it on purpose, update STANDARDS in this script"
		fi
		;;
	esac
fi
SECTION='Answering a finding'
if ! grep -q "^### $SECTION" "$AGENTS"; then
	fail "AGENTS.md has no '### $SECTION' section -- step 6 points at it by name, and it is where the standard the three steps state is defined"
fi
# And the pointer to it, which is the one thing tying the numbered steps
# to the definition. Delete just that clause and the count above still
# reads 4 and the heading is still there: the section goes on existing
# with nothing sending a reader to it, which loses the half of #97 that
# asked where a disagreement is recorded. Matched in quotes because the
# heading itself is unquoted, so this finds the reference and not the
# thing referred to.
if ! grep -q "\"$SECTION\"" "$AGENTS"; then
	fail "nothing in AGENTS.md refers to \"$SECTION\" -- the section defines the standard steps 6, 7 and 8 state, and nothing now sends a reader to it"
fi

# CLAUDE.md points at it and holds nothing else.
if ! grep -q '^@AGENTS\.md[[:space:]]*$' "$CLAUDE"; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md has no '@AGENTS.md' import line -- Claude Code would not load the shared rules"
fi
# Blank out the one allowed import and see if any other remains. An
# import works mid-line too, so matching only at the start of a line
# would miss `... see @RULES.md:` -- four lines, small, and a second
# source of truth in every session. Only whole tokens are blanked, or
# `@AGENTS.md.bak` would be read as the allowed import plus nothing --
# and since `.` has to count as part of a token for that, sentence
# punctuation after the import is absorbed too.
if sed -E 's#@AGENTS\.md([.,;:!?]?)([^A-Za-z0-9._/-]|$)#\1\2#g' "$CLAUDE" \
		| grep -q '@[A-Za-z0-9._/-]'; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md imports a file other than AGENTS.md -- rules should reach agents through AGENTS.md alone"
fi
if [ "$claudebytes" -gt "$MAXBYTES" ]; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md is $claudebytes bytes, over the $MAXBYTES limit -- rules belong in AGENTS.md, not here"
fi

claudelines=$(grep -cv '^[[:space:]]*$' "$CLAUDE")
if [ "$claudelines" -gt "$MAXLINES" ]; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md has $claudelines non-blank lines, expected at most $MAXLINES -- if you added a rule, move it to AGENTS.md; if you reworded the pointer, update MAXLINES in this script"
fi

# Rules arrive as list items or new sections. The pointer needs neither,
# so their presence below the title means content landed in the wrong file.
if tail -n +2 "$CLAUDE" | grep -qE '^[[:space:]]*(#|[-*+][[:space:]]|[0-9]+\.[[:space:]])'; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md contains headings or list items below the title -- move that content to AGENTS.md"
fi

# Claude Code also loads CLAUDE.md files from subdirectories (when working
# under them) and from .claude/. Any of those is a second shared source of
# truth, so only the root pointer may exist. A personal, unshared
# CLAUDE.local.md at the root is deliberately left alone -- .gitignore
# keeps it from becoming a shared one.
#
# Matched case-insensitively: macOS filesystems are case-insensitive by
# default, so a lone claude.md there would load like the real thing.
# The prune list mirrors .gitignore's build trees rather than any
# directory merely starting with "build".
extra=$(find "$ROOT" \( -name .git -o -name build -o -name 'build-*' \) -prune -o \
	-iname 'CLAUDE*.md' \

#!/bin/sh
# Checks that AGENTS.md stays the single source of truth for project
# instructions, and that CLAUDE.md stays a pointer to it.
#
# Rules drift into CLAUDE.md easily and silently: Claude Code's `#`
# shortcut appends there, `/init` rewrites the file wholesale, and
# tools that target CLAUDE.md by name edit it directly. None of them
# know AGENTS.md exists. Without a check, the result is two sources of
# truth that slowly disagree.
#
# The AGENTS.md checks matter just as much: CLAUDE.md pulls it in with
# an `@AGENTS.md` import, and if that file is renamed, emptied, or
# deleted the import resolves to nothing -- no error, no warning, just
# an agent session with no rules at all.
#
# Usage: instructions.sh /path/to/repo/root

set -u

ROOT="${1:-.}"
while [ "${ROOT%/}" != "$ROOT" ] && [ "$ROOT" != "/" ]; do
	ROOT="${ROOT%/}"
done
CLAUDE="$ROOT/CLAUDE.md"
AGENTS="$ROOT/AGENTS.md"

# The pointer needs a title, a sentence or two, and the import. Kept
# tight on purpose: headroom here is room for a rule to hide by being
# folded into an existing line rather than added as a new one, which
# the line budget below cannot see. A very short phrase can still fit;
# that one is left to review.
MAXBYTES=220
# CLAUDE.md is meant to be frozen, so this is the exact number of
# non-blank lines it has today, not a generous budget: a rule slipped in
# as plain prose adds a line and nothing else would. Changing the
# pointer's wording means changing this number on purpose. The prose is
# wrapped at 72 columns to match the rest of the repo -- rewrapping it
# much narrower will need a third line and trip this.
MAXLINES=4
# Enough that a gutted or stub AGENTS.md fails, well under its real size.
MINAGENTS=2000

fails=0
fail() {
	printf 'FAIL: %s\n' "$1" >&2
	fails=$((fails + 1))
}

if [ ! -f "$AGENTS" ]; then
	fail "AGENTS.md is missing -- CLAUDE.md's @AGENTS.md import would silently resolve to nothing"
fi
if [ ! -f "$CLAUDE" ]; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md is missing -- Claude Code sessions would load no project rules"
fi
if [ "$fails" -ne 0 ]; then
	exit 1
fi

agentsbytes=$(wc -c < "$AGENTS" | tr -d ' ')
claudebytes=$(wc -c < "$CLAUDE" | tr -d ' ')

# AGENTS.md holds the real content.
if [ "$agentsbytes" -lt "$MINAGENTS" ]; then
	fail "AGENTS.md is only $agentsbytes bytes; expected at least $MINAGENTS -- has its content been moved or lost?"
fi
if ! grep -q '^## Development workflow' "$AGENTS"; then
	fail "AGENTS.md has no '## Development workflow' section -- the workflow every agent follows should live there"
fi

# Steps 6, 7 and 8 hold their review passes to one standard, and say it
# in one form of words so a reader can see that they agree. They did not
# always: two said "address every actionable finding" and the middle one
# said "fix or explicitly resolve", while the first claimed to be
# stating the same rule "as with the two steps below". Nobody noticed
# until a reviewer read all three together.
#
# Counted, not located: hard-coding line numbers would break on every
# edit above them, and nothing here can tell which step a match fell in.
# So this catches the one-place regression -- a step reworded on its own
# -- and not a coordinated edit that reworded a step and added the
# phrase somewhere else to keep the total at four. Issue #65 is the
# check that would know one step from another.
#
# Counted over the file with its line breaks flattened, because the
# phrase wraps mid-sentence in two of the four places it appears: a
# check a rewrap can break is a check that gets deleted the first time
# someone rewraps. The phrase holds no regex metacharacter, so passing
# it to awk as a pattern matches it literally; one added later would
# quietly turn this into something else.
STANDARD='actionable finding, or resolve it explicitly'
# Three steps state it and one section defines it. Stating it a fifth
# time on purpose means changing this number on purpose.
STANDARDS=4
# Awk's status and its output are both checked, because either can lie
# on its own. A non-number means it did not run -- unsupported construct,
# missing binary, anything -- and compared directly against STANDARDS
# that is a silent pass rather than a failure: the test errors "Illegal
# number", `if` reads the non-zero status as false, and the script goes
# on to print "instructions OK". A number from a command that then
# failed is the same hole from the other side: a shadowed awk printing
# "4" and exiting 17 satisfied the number check, and did it on a file
# whose step 8 had been reworded back to the old standard -- green,
# with the defect present and the counter never having run.
if ! standards=$(awk -v want="$STANDARD" '
	{ s = s " " $0 }
	END { gsub(/[ \t]+/, " ", s); print gsub(want, "&", s) }' "$AGENTS"); then
	fail "could not count the finding standard in AGENTS.md -- awk exited non-zero, so this check did not run whatever it printed"
else
	case "$standards" in
	'' | *[!0-9]*)
		fail "could not count the finding standard in AGENTS.md -- awk printed '$standards' instead of a number, so this check did not run"
		;;
	*)
		if [ "$standards" -ne "$STANDARDS" ]; then
			fail "AGENTS.md states the finding standard $standards times, expected $STANDARDS -- steps 6, 7 and 8 each state it and 'Answering a finding' defines it. A step reworded on its own no longer visibly agrees with the others; if you added a statement of it on purpose, update STANDARDS in this script"
		fi
		;;
	esac
fi
SECTION='Answering a finding'
if ! grep -q "^### $SECTION" "$AGENTS"; then
	fail "AGENTS.md has no '### $SECTION' section -- step 6 points at it by name, and it is where the standard the three steps state is defined"
fi
# And the pointer to it, which is the one thing tying the numbered steps
# to the definition. Delete just that clause and the count above still
# reads 4 and the heading is still there: the section goes on existing
# with nothing sending a reader to it, which loses the half of #97 that
# asked where a disagreement is recorded. Matched in quotes because the
# heading itself is unquoted, so this finds the reference and not the
# thing referred to.
if ! grep -q "\"$SECTION\"" "$AGENTS"; then
	fail "nothing in AGENTS.md refers to \"$SECTION\" -- the section defines the standard steps 6, 7 and 8 state, and nothing now sends a reader to it"
fi

# CLAUDE.md points at it and holds nothing else.
if ! grep -q '^@AGENTS\.md[[:space:]]*$' "$CLAUDE"; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md has no '@AGENTS.md' import line -- Claude Code would not load the shared rules"
fi
# Blank out the one allowed import and see if any other remains. An
# import works mid-line too, so matching only at the start of a line
# would miss `... see @RULES.md:` -- four lines, small, and a second
# source of truth in every session. Only whole tokens are blanked, or
# `@AGENTS.md.bak` would be read as the allowed import plus nothing --
# and since `.` has to count as part of a token for that, sentence
# punctuation after the import is absorbed too.
if sed -E 's#@AGENTS\.md([.,;:!?]?)([^A-Za-z0-9._/-]|$)#\1\2#g' "$CLAUDE" \
		| grep -q '@[A-Za-z0-9._/-]'; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md imports a file other than AGENTS.md -- rules should reach agents through AGENTS.md alone"
fi
if [ "$claudebytes" -gt "$MAXBYTES" ]; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md is $claudebytes bytes, over the $MAXBYTES limit -- rules belong in AGENTS.md, not here"
fi

claudelines=$(grep -cv '^[[:space:]]*$' "$CLAUDE")
if [ "$claudelines" -gt "$MAXLINES" ]; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md has $claudelines non-blank lines, expected at most $MAXLINES -- if you added a rule, move it to AGENTS.md; if you reworded the pointer, update MAXLINES in this script"
fi

# Rules arrive as list items or new sections. The pointer needs neither,
# so their presence below the title means content landed in the wrong file.
if tail -n +2 "$CLAUDE" | grep -qE '^[[:space:]]*(#|[-*+][[:space:]]|[0-9]+\.[[:space:]])'; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md contains headings or list items below the title -- move that content to AGENTS.md"
fi

# Claude Code also loads CLAUDE.md files from subdirectories (when working
# under them) and from .claude/. Any of those is a second shared source of
# truth, so only the root pointer may exist. A personal, unshared
# CLAUDE.local.md at the root is deliberately left alone -- .gitignore
# keeps it from becoming a shared one.
#
# Matched case-insensitively: macOS filesystems are case-insensitive by
# default, so a lone claude.md there would load like the real thing.
# The prune list mirrors .gitignore's build trees rather than any
# directory merely starting with "build".
extra=$(find "$ROOT" \( -name .git -o -name build -o -name 'build-*' \) -prune -o \
	-iname 'CLAUDE*.md' \
	! -ipath "$ROOT/CLAUDE.md" \
	! -ipath "$ROOT/CLAUDE.local.md" \
	-print 2>/dev/null)
if [ -n "$extra" ]; then
	fail "these files also carry instructions; fold them into AGENTS.md:"
	echo "$extra" | sed 's/^/         /' >&2
fi

if [ "$fails" -ne 0 ]; then
	printf '\n%d check(s) failed.\n' "$fails" >&2
	printf 'AGENTS.md is the source of truth for every coding agent; CLAUDE.md only imports it.\n' >&2
	printf 'Put project rules in AGENTS.md and leave CLAUDE.md as the pointer.\n' >&2
	exit 1
fi

printf 'instructions OK (CLAUDE.md %s bytes, AGENTS.md %s bytes)\n' "$claudebytes" "$agentsbytes"

Both applied verbatim. Please re-read `AGENTS.md` and `tests/instructions.sh` from the repository and give a verdict.

**1. The disjunction.** Now:

> Either way it goes in the pull request body and in the summary of the work — in the summary alone when there is no pull request, on the same terms steps 3 and 9 already set. A resolution nobody can find afterwards is the silence this rule exists to stop.

I took your wording and also cut the trailing clause I had ("and a task with no pull request is where that is easiest to reach by accident") — it was arguing for the fallback, which the sentence now simply states, and your failure scenario is the one that matters: the case with a PR, where the summary was being dropped.

You were right that this reproduced the branch's own motivating bug. That is the fifth claim about numbered steps in this change and the fourth to come back wrong, which is worth saying plainly rather than quietly fixing — a rate like that is the argument for the check the script now carries, not against it.

**2. The #65 pointer.** Your clause verbatim: "Issue #65 is where that check would live -- as filed it checks numbering, not which step a match fell in; the comment thread there asks for the attribution it would need." Your reading is right that it was *as well as*, not instead — the issue comment keeps straight who said what, and the script comment is what a maintainer actually reads.

Verified: `shellcheck` clean, `tests/instructions.sh` green, `ctest -R instructions` green, phrase count still 4 (the edit touched neither the counted phrase nor `STANDARDS`).

One thing to check rather than confirm: **the paragraph is now the longest in the section**, and it carries four destinations — the next pass, the PR body, the summary, and the summary-alone fallback. I would rather it be a rule someone follows than complete. If the "where it goes" paragraph should be split or shortened now that the conjunction made it longer, say so; that is the sort of thing I would not notice having rewritten it four times.

Both Codex findings were real, and both were holes in work that had already passed three reviewers.

**The first is the one worth telling you about.** My awk guard — added specifically to close a silent-pass hole — had a silent-pass hole of its own: it validated awk's *output* and never its *exit status*. `code-review`, the `verifier` and I each built a fake-awk matrix; none of us tried an awk that prints a valid answer and then fails. The guard masked the exact defect the check exists to catch.

**The second** was a missing fallback — a resolved finding had nowhere to go when work ends without a PR, though the file has that fallback in steps 3 and 9.

Fixing the second then produced a *third* defect of the same family: I wrote "PR body **or** summary" while the steps I cited set "PR body **and** summary." That's five claims about numbered steps in this change and four of them came back wrong — which is the argument for the check the script now carries.

Waiting on the final `code-review` verdict. Once it's clean I'll commit, push to #99, and resolve the two Codex threads — then **stop before merging**, as you asked.

`tests/instructions.sh .` green, `ctest -R instructions` green, `git diff --check` clean.

Your reading of the paragraph was better than mine: I had counted destinations, and there are two rules — route it if a pass runs anyway, write it down either way. The break puts the unconditional one at the head of its own paragraph, and "Either way" still refers back correctly across the break.

I am also taking your note about where the rate gets said. The commit body will carry it: that this change made five claims about numbered steps and four came back wrong, and — the part worth being explicit about — that the check catches one of those five shapes, a step reworded on its own, and nothing about a prose citation to a step. A reader who sees a test guarding "step references" should not conclude the citations are guarded, because they are not.

If that hunk is what you expect, say so and I will commit. If the break landed somewhere other than where you meant it, say that instead.

content.content:
fix(tui): clip the panels by row as well as by column (#96)

#78 bounded the panel draw loops by column. Nothing bounded them by
row, and tui_refresh_panels() asks for all eleven lines however short
the terminal is. Two ways to fail, one on each side of the last row: at
twelve rows the tenth grid line was drawn onto the bottom border, and
at eleven wmove() failed outright, left the cursor where the previous
line had left it, and the whole line landed on the row above --
`mq 9  . . . . . . . . . .10 .x`, two grid rows and a border sharing
one line.

panel_has_row() asks what panel_room() asks on the other axis, and both
draw loops return early when the row is not inside the box. That alone
fixed the quadrant panel and not the status panel, which turned out to
be a second defect: make_windows() resized the status panel back to its
full PANELH rows on every repaint whatever the screen height, so it
stayed taller than the screen, its bottom border fell off the bottom,
and its last line was drawn where that border should have been. It now
takes the height the screen can show, as the quadrant panel already did
by way of resize_term().

input.content:
docs: check awk's status, and record a resolution without a PR

Two findings from the Codex review of #99, both real.

The guard added to close a silent-pass hole had one of its own. It
validated awk's output and never its exit status, so an awk that
printed a valid count and then failed satisfied it. Worse than that
sounds: a stub printing "4" and exiting 17 made the script print
"instructions OK" on a file whose step 8 had been reworded back to the
old standard -- the guard masking the exact defect the check exists to
catch. Three fake-awk matrices had been built for this check by then,
by three different readers, and none of them tried an awk that succeeds
and then fails.

And a resolved finding had nowhere to go when the work ends without a
pull request. Steps 3 and 9 set that fallback -- the summary alone --
and the new section named only the pull request body.

Fixing the second produced a third defect of the same family, caught in
review: the sentence read "pull request body or summary" where the
steps it cited set "and", with summary alone as the fallback. That is
five claims about numbered steps in this change and four of them came
back wrong.

Worth being exact about what the check in tests/instructions.sh covers,
given that rate. It catches one of those five shapes -- a step reworded
on its own so the standard is no longer stated three times -- and
nothing at all about whether a sentence describing a step describes it
correctly. A reader who sees a test guarding step references should not
conclude the citations are guarded. They are not, and #65 is where the
check that could know one step from another would live.

Closes #97

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
